points.guide: The change in internal energy as given by ΔU = (3/2)Nk_BΔT = (3/2)nRΔT of a system is related to the change of its temperature.
aims: Describe internal energy, and distinguish it from heat and work.
Calculate the change in internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas from its change in temperature.

slides.title: What is internal energy?
bullets: Internal energy $U$: the total random kinetic energy of the particles plus the potential energy of the forces between them
In an ideal gas the particles exert no forces except in collisions, so its internal energy is all kinetic
The mean kinetic energy of a particle is proportional to the kelvin temperature (B.3)
Exam calculations on gases in B.4 use monatomic ideal gases, such as helium, neon and argon
A positive $\Delta U$ means the internal energy has increased; a negative one means it has decreased
slides.notes: Gases with more than one atom per molecule also store energy in rotation and vibration, so they need more energy for the same temperature rise. That is beyond the calculations here, but worth saying once. The examples here with air or steam use only the first law and $W = P\Delta V$, which hold for any gas.

slides.title: Heat is not internal energy
bullets: Internal energy is something a system has; heat and work are ways of transferring energy
Heat (thermal energy transfer): energy moving because of a temperature difference
Work: energy transferred by a force acting through a distance, such as a gas pushing a piston
Energy supplied may raise the mean kinetic energy (the temperature rises) or stretch bonds (raising potential energy at constant temperature, as in melting)
Avoid saying that a body "contains heat"
slides.notes: The comparison with mechanics helps: work is not "stored" in a body either. It is a transfer into or out of a store.

slides.title: Change in internal energy
bullets: Use $N$ (number of atoms) with $k_B$, and $n$ (amount in moles) with $R$
For a fixed amount of monatomic ideal gas, $U$ depends only on the temperature
slides.notes: Both forms are in the data booklet. $k_B = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\ \text{J K}^{-1}$ and $R = 8.31\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$.

slides.title: Deriving the internal energy change
slides.start: Start from the mean kinetic energy of one atom (B.3). The atoms of a monatomic ideal gas have no potential energy.

steps.text: Mean kinetic energy of one atom
Multiply by the number of atoms $N$
Only $T$ can change, for a fixed amount of gas
Since $N = nN_A$ and $R = N_Ak_B$, the product $Nk_B$ equals $nR$
From $PV = nRT$: useful when given $P$ and $V$

slides.notes: The last line isn't in the data booklet, but it saves a lot of time on p–V cycle questions.

slides.title: A welding cylinder in the sun
slides.question: A sealed steel welding cylinder holds 80 mol of argon, a monatomic gas. Standing in the sun, it warms from 288 K to 313 K. Find the increase in internal energy of the argon, (a) using $n$ and $R$ and (b) using $N$ and $k_B$.
slides.hint: Find the temperature change first. Then choose the form of the equation that matches the quantity you are using, moles or atoms.

steps.text: Use atoms and $k_B$: the same result

slides.notes: The cylinder's volume is fixed, so no work is done, and all of this energy arrived by heating.

points.guide: The first law of thermodynamics as given by Q = ΔU + W results from the application of conservation of energy to a closed system and relates the internal energy of a system to the transfer of energy as heat and as work. (Guidance: closed and isolated systems; Clausius sign convention.)
aims: Distinguish between closed and isolated systems, and use the Clausius sign convention for $Q$ and $W$.
Apply the first law $Q = \Delta U + W$ to a gas.

slides.title: Systems and signs
bullets: Closed system: no mass enters or leaves, but energy can transfer as heat or as work
Isolated system: neither mass nor energy can enter or leave
Clausius sign convention:
$Q$ is positive when thermal energy goes into the system
$W$ is positive when the system does work on its surroundings
So work done on a gas (a compression) makes $W$ negative
slides.notes: A gas in a syringe being heated is closed, not isolated. Ask students for one everyday example of each.

slides.title: The first law of thermodynamics
bullets: Conservation of energy for a closed system
Thermal energy supplied goes into raising the internal energy and into work done by the gas
slides.notes: Some older books define $W$ as the work done on the gas, which changes a sign in the law. The IB uses the form above.

slides.title: Using the first law
bullets: Rewrite it as $\Delta U = Q - W$ when you want the change in internal energy
Decide the sign of $Q$ and of $W$ before you substitute
"Loses energy to the surroundings" means a negative $Q$
"Is compressed" or "work is done on it" means a negative $W$
The law holds for any closed system; only $\Delta U = \tfrac{3}{2}nR\Delta T$ needs a monatomic ideal gas

slides.title: A bicycle pump
slides.question: During one stroke of a bicycle pump, with the outlet closed, 18 J of work is done on the air in the barrel, and the air loses 5 J of thermal energy to the barrel walls. Find the change in internal energy of the air.
slides.hint: Work out the sign of each term first. Is energy leaving or entering as heat? Is the air doing work, or having work done on it?

steps.text: Work is done on the air, so $W$ is negative
The air loses thermal energy, so $Q$ is negative
The internal energy rises, so the air warms

slides.notes: Students who have pumped a tyre will know the barrel gets warm.

slides.title: The power stroke
slides.question: During the power stroke in one cylinder of a car engine, the hot gas does 420 J of work on the piston, and 150 J of thermal energy passes from the gas into the cylinder walls. Find the change in internal energy of the gas, and state what happens to its temperature.
slides.hint: Here the gas does work and also loses thermal energy. Decide what that means for the signs of $W$ and $Q$.

steps.text: The gas does work on the piston
Energy leaves the gas as heat
The internal energy falls, so the temperature falls

points.guide: The work done by or on a closed system as given by W = PΔV when its boundaries are changed can be described in terms of pressure and changes of volume of the system. (Guidance: includes situations where pressure is not constant.)
aims: Calculate the work done by or on a gas at constant pressure using $W = P\Delta V$.
Find the work done when the pressure changes, from the area under a p–V graph.

slides.title: When a gas changes volume
bullets: A gas pushes on the walls of its container, so a moving wall has work done on it
Expanding gas ($\Delta V$ positive): the gas does work, so $W$ is positive
Compressed gas ($\Delta V$ negative): work is done on the gas, so $W$ is negative
No change in volume: no work is done
When the pressure changes, the work is the area under the p–V graph

slides.title: Work done by a gas
bullets: Valid when the pressure is constant
Pressure in pascals and volume in $\text{m}^{3}$ give work in joules
slides.notes: $1\ \text{litre} = 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3$ and $1\ \text{cm}^3 = 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^3$: unit changes are the commonest source of lost marks here.

slides.title: Deriving the work done by a gas
slides.start: A gas at constant pressure $P$ pushes a piston of area $A$ out through a short distance $d$.

steps.text: Force of the gas on the piston
The volume swept out by the piston
Substitute: the work done by the gas

slides.title: Work is the area under the graph
bullets: The area has units of $\text{Pa} \times \text{m}^{3} = \text{J}$
A straight sloping line gives a trapezium
A curve: count squares on the grid

slides.title: A steam engine cylinder
slides.question: While the inlet valve of a steam engine is open, steam at a constant pressure of $4.0 \times 10^{5}$ Pa pushes a piston of area 0.080 $\text{m}^{2}$ through a distance of 0.60 m. Find the work done by the steam.
slides.hint: The pressure is constant. Find the change in volume from the area of the piston and how far it moves.

steps.text: Volume swept out by the piston
The work done by the steam

slides.notes: A good moment to raise the guide's linking question about harnessing the power of steam.

slides.title: An air shock on a mountain bike
slides.question: As the air shock on a mountain bike extends, the volume of the air inside rises from $1.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^{3}$ to $1.5 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^{3}$, while the pressure falls from $1.2 \times 10^{6}$ Pa to $0.80 \times 10^{6}$ Pa. Taking the p–V graph to be a straight line, find the work done by the air.
slides.hint: The pressure isn't constant, so sketch the graph. What shape is the region under a sloping straight line?

steps.text: The area under the line is a trapezium: use the mean pressure
Area = mean pressure × change in volume

points.guide: Isovolumetric, isobaric, isothermal and adiabatic processes are obtained by keeping one variable fixed.
aims: Identify isovolumetric, isobaric, isothermal and adiabatic processes, in words and on p–V graphs.
Apply the first law to each type of process.

slides.title: States and processes
bullets: The state of a gas is its set of values of $P$, $V$, $n$ and $T$, linked by $PV = nRT$
A process takes the gas from one state to another
With $n$ fixed, four simple processes each hold one thing fixed:
isovolumetric (isochoric): constant volume
isobaric: constant pressure
isothermal: constant temperature
adiabatic: no thermal energy transfer
slides.notes: When measuring these changes in the lab, wait before each reading: the gas must return to the temperature of its bath if the change is to count as isothermal.

slides.title: Sketching processes on a p–V graph
bullets: Isovolumetric: a vertical line; isobaric: a horizontal line
Isothermal: a curve called an isotherm, with $P$ inversely proportional to $V$
A higher temperature gives an isotherm further from the origin
Moving between isotherms tells you whether the gas is warming or cooling
Put an arrow on each line to show the direction of the change
slides.notes: Pressure, volume and temperature can be drawn as a 3D surface. Each isotherm is one slice through it at a fixed temperature.

slides.title: Four processes from one point
slides.alt: A pressure against volume graph with four paths from the point A. Isochoric: straight up at constant volume. Isobaric: horizontally to the right at constant pressure. Isothermal: a curve falling to the right. Adiabatic: a steeper curve falling to the right, below the isothermal curve.
bullets: Isochoric: constant $V$ (vertical)
Isobaric: constant $P$ (horizontal)
Isothermal: constant $T$
Adiabatic: $Q = 0$, so steeper than the isothermal
slides.notes: The curves are calculated for a monatomic ideal gas: isothermal $PV = $ constant, adiabatic $PV^{5/3} = $ constant. Ask which expansion does the most work, by comparing the areas under the paths.

slides.title: The first law in each process
bullets: Each one comes from fixing one quantity in the first law, $Q = \Delta U + W$
The isothermal form needs an ideal gas, for which constant temperature means $\Delta U = 0$
slides.notes: Only the first law itself and $W = P\Delta V$ are in the data booklet. Students should be able to produce these four forms quickly.

slides.title: The gas laws from the equation of state
slides.start: Start from $PV = nRT$ with $n$ and $R$ constant, then hold one more quantity fixed.
slides.notes: Each of these needs a closed system, because $n$ is fixed. It need not be isolated: energy must flow in or out for most of these changes.

slides.title: Absolute zero from a pressure graph
slides.start: A fixed amount of gas at constant volume is warmed. Its Celsius temperature $\theta$ and pressure $P$ are recorded.

steps.text: A straight line on a graph of $P$ against $\theta$, not through the origin
The pressure would reach zero at the intercept: absolute zero

slides.title: Thermal energy at constant pressure
slides.start: A monatomic ideal gas changes temperature at constant pressure. Find the work done and the thermal energy needed.

steps.text: The change in internal energy is
Add these, by the first law
So the thermal energy transferred is

slides.notes: At constant volume, the thermal energy needed for the same temperature rise is only $\tfrac{3}{2}nR\Delta T$, because no work is done.

slides.title: Switching on a filament lamp
slides.question: A filament lamp of internal volume $1.2 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^{3}$ is filled with argon (treated as a monatomic ideal gas) at $8.0 \times 10^{4}$ Pa and 295 K. When it is switched on, the mean temperature of the argon rises to 400 K. Find (a) the new pressure of the argon and (b) the thermal energy absorbed by the argon.
slides.hint: The glass doesn't change size, so this is an isovolumetric change. What does that make $W$? In (b), $\Delta U = \tfrac{3}{2}\Delta(PV)$ avoids finding $n$.

steps.text: (a) At constant volume, pressure is proportional to $T$
The unrounded pressure rise is $2.85 \times 10^{4}$ Pa

slides.notes: Lamp makers choose a filling pressure below atmospheric so that the pressure is close to atmospheric when the lamp is hot.

slides.title: Slow compression in a water bath
slides.question: Krypton (treated as a monatomic ideal gas) in a thin metal cylinder stands in a water bath and is compressed very slowly, from $2.4 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^{3}$ at $1.1 \times 10^{5}$ Pa to $0.80 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^{3}$. The work done on the krypton is 29 J. Find (a) its final pressure, (b) the change in its internal energy and (c) the thermal energy transferred, stating the direction.
slides.hint: Slow compression in a water bath keeps the temperature constant. What does that tell you about $PV$, and about $\Delta U$?

steps.text: (c) Work is done on the gas, so $W$ is negative
So 29 J of thermal energy leaves the krypton and passes to the water.

points.guide: Adiabatic processes in monatomic ideal gases can be modelled by the equation as given by PV^(5/3) = constant.
aims: Explain why a gas cools in an adiabatic expansion and warms in an adiabatic compression.
Use $PV^{\frac{5}{3}} = \text{constant}$ for a monatomic ideal gas.

slides.title: Adiabatic changes
bullets: In an adiabatic process no thermal energy enters or leaves, so $Q = 0$ and $\Delta U = -W$
This happens when the gas is well insulated, or when the change is so fast that heat has no time to flow
Expanding: the gas does work out of its own internal energy, and cools
Compressed: the work done on the gas goes into its internal energy, and it warms
slides.notes: Quick demonstration: a fire syringe. Air compressed very quickly becomes hot enough to light a scrap of cotton wool.

slides.title: Isothermal or adiabatic?
bullets: Isothermal: the temperature is fixed, and thermal energy transfers ($Q = W$)
Adiabatic: no thermal energy transfers, and the temperature changes ($\Delta U = -W$)
Isothermal needs a slow change, with good thermal contact
Adiabatic needs a fast change, or good insulation
In an adiabatic compression the pressure rises for two reasons: smaller volume and higher temperature

slides.title: Adiabatic change
bullets: Only for a monatomic ideal gas
Between two states, the product is the same at each end
Given without proof at this level; it is in the data booklet
slides.notes: Strictly, the equation describes a reversible adiabatic change, with a well-defined pressure throughout. A gas rushing freely into a vacuum has $Q = 0$ but does not follow it.

slides.title: Temperature in an adiabatic change
slides.start: For a monatomic ideal gas, combine the adiabatic equation with the equation of state, to remove the pressure.
slides.notes: Students can always reach the same answer with $PV/T = \text{constant}$ as a second step, so this form is a convenience and not something to memorise. Like the adiabatic equation, it holds only for a monatomic ideal gas, and it is not in the data booklet.

slides.title: An adiabat is steeper than an isotherm
bullets: Both curves pass through the same state
Compressing along the adiabat gives a higher pressure, because the gas also warms

slides.title: Inside a cryocooler
slides.question: In a cryocooler, used to chill sensitive detectors, helium (treated as a monatomic ideal gas) at $2.0 \times 10^{6}$ Pa and 60 K expands adiabatically until its pressure is $5.0 \times 10^{5}$ Pa. Find (a) the factor by which its volume increases and (b) its final temperature.
slides.hint: Write the adiabatic equation for the two states and make the volume ratio the subject. For the temperature, you can use $\dfrac{PV}{T} = \text{constant}$.

steps.text: (a) Rearrange the adiabatic equation for the two states
(b) Use the ideal gas relation, with the unrounded ratio

slides.notes: Helium is used because it stays a gas at these very low temperatures.

slides.title: A rapid compression machine
slides.question: Rapid compression machines are used to study how fuels ignite. In one, 0.040 mol of argon (treated as a monatomic ideal gas) at 310 K is squeezed adiabatically to one fifth of its original volume. Find (a) the final temperature and (b) the work done by the argon.
slides.hint: The form of the adiabatic equation with $T$ and $V$ gets straight to the temperature. Then use the first law: what is $Q$?

steps.text: This is the change in internal energy
Adiabatic, so $Q = 0$ and the work is the negative of this

slides.notes: The negative sign means work is done on the gas. Argon reaches a higher temperature than air would for the same compression.

points.guide: Cyclic gas processes are used to run heat engines.
aims: Describe how a cycle of gas processes runs a heat engine.
Find the net work done in a cycle from a p–V graph, and explain what reversing the cycle does.

slides.title: Cycles on a p–V graph
bullets: A cycle is a series of processes that brings the gas back to its starting state
The temperature returns to its first value, so $\Delta U = 0$ over a whole cycle
So over a cycle the net thermal energy in equals the net work out
Net work per cycle = area enclosed by the loop
Clockwise loop: the gas does net work (an engine)
slides.notes: Ask why more work is done by the gas than on it in a clockwise loop: the expansion happens at higher pressures than the compression.

slides.title: Heat engines
bullets: A heat engine converts part of the thermal energy it takes in into mechanical work, cycle after cycle
Simplest form: a gas in a cylinder with a piston
It takes in thermal energy from a hot reservoir (for example, burning fuel)
It does useful work on the piston
It gives out the rest to a cold reservoir (for example, the air or a river)
slides.notes: Show an animation of a four-stroke engine and ask students to pick out each stage of the cycle.

slides.title: Running a cycle backwards
bullets: An anticlockwise loop means net work is done on the gas
The gas takes in thermal energy at low temperature and gives it out at high temperature
Reversing the cycle changes the sign of the net work, not its size
This is how refrigerators and heat pumps work
Energy can move from cold to hot here only because work is done on the system
slides.notes: For a fridge, the energy given out to the kitchen equals the energy removed from the food compartment plus the work done by the compressor. Students rarely expect that the kitchen ends up warmer.

slides.title: Energy flows in a refrigerator
slides.alt: Energy flow diagram. Thermal energy Q c flows from the cold interior into the fridge. Work W is done on the fridge. Thermal energy Q h flows out of the fridge to the hot surroundings.
bullets: Work $W$ moves thermal energy from cold to hot
Energy is conserved: $Q_{\text{h}} = Q_{\text{c}} + W$
With no work this would be impossible: the second law
slides.notes: A fridge is a heat engine run backwards. Compare the arrows with the heat engine diagram: every one is reversed.

slides.title: A four-stage cycle
slides.question: The gas in a model engine goes round the cycle A → B → C → D → A in straight lines. In pascals and $\text{m}^{3}$, the states are A $(2.0 \times 10^{5},\ 1.0 \times 10^{-3})$, B $(2.0 \times 10^{5},\ 4.0 \times 10^{-3})$, C $(1.0 \times 10^{5},\ 3.0 \times 10^{-3})$ and D $(1.0 \times 10^{5},\ 1.0 \times 10^{-3})$. Find the work done in each stage and the net work per cycle.
slides.hint: Sketch the cycle first. Which stages are at constant pressure, and which is at constant volume? B → C is a sloping line, so use the area under it.

steps.text: So A → B gives $W = +600$ J. B → C: use the mean pressure of $1.5 \times 10^{5}$ Pa
So C → D gives $W = -200$ J, and D → A has no volume change. Add them

slides.notes: Check with the enclosed area: a trapezium with parallel sides $3.0 \times 10^{-3}$ and $2.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3$ and height $1.0 \times 10^{5}$ Pa has area 250 J.

points.guide: A heat engine can respond to different cycles and is characterized by its efficiency as given by η = useful work / input energy.
aims: Calculate the efficiency of a heat engine from energy transfers.
Find the input energy of a gas cycle from the first law.

slides.title: Comparing engines
bullets: Engines can run on different cycles: petrol engines, diesel engines and Stirling engines all use different ones
Whatever the cycle, an engine is rated by its efficiency
Efficiency compares the useful work with the thermal energy taken in
The energy given out to the cold reservoir isn't useful, but it can't be avoided

slides.title: Efficiency of a heat engine
bullets: No unit; often given as a percentage
The work per cycle is $Q_h - Q_c$: energy from the hot reservoir minus energy to the cold one

slides.title: Efficiency from the energy flows
slides.start: Over one full cycle the gas returns to its starting state. Let $Q_h$ and $Q_c$ be the sizes of the two energy transfers.

steps.text: The internal energy returns to its first value
The first law: net thermal energy in equals work

slides.title: Finding the efficiency of a cycle
bullets: For each stage, find $W$ (area under the line) and $\Delta U$ (from $\tfrac{3}{2}\Delta(PV)$)
Then use the first law to find $Q$ for each stage
Only the stages with positive $Q$ count towards the input energy
Check: the sum of all the values of $Q$ should equal the net work

slides.title: The energy flow in a heat engine
bullets: The arrows are not drawn to scale
Only the work is a useful output

slides.title: A steam locomotive
slides.question: A steam locomotive burns coal, releasing thermal energy at a rate of 12 MW, and delivers a useful power of 0.90 MW. Find (a) its efficiency and (b) the rate at which it rejects thermal energy. (c) The specific energy of the coal is $30\ \text{MJ kg}^{-1}$. Find the mass of coal burned in one hour.
slides.hint: Efficiency works with rates of energy transfer just as it does with energies. What happens to the energy that doesn't become useful work?
slides.notes: Despite this low efficiency, steam power changed society. A good link to the guide's NoS linking question.

slides.title: The efficiency of a model engine
slides.question: A model engine contains a monatomic ideal gas, which goes round the cycle A → B → C → D → A in straight lines. In pascals and $\text{m}^{3}$, its states are A $(2.0 \times 10^{5},\ 1.0 \times 10^{-3})$, B $(2.0 \times 10^{5},\ 4.0 \times 10^{-3})$, C $(1.0 \times 10^{5},\ 3.0 \times 10^{-3})$ and D $(1.0 \times 10^{5},\ 1.0 \times 10^{-3})$. The net work per cycle is 250 J. Find the efficiency of the engine.
slides.hint: Use $\Delta U = \tfrac{3}{2}\Delta(PV)$ and the work done in each stage, then apply the first law to each. Which stages take in thermal energy?

steps.text: A → B: $PV$ rises from 200 J to 800 J, so $\Delta U = 900$ J; $W = 600$ J
B → C: $PV$ falls to 300 J, so $\Delta U = -750$ J; $W = -150$ J
C → D: $PV$ falls to 100 J, so $\Delta U = -300$ J; $W = -200$ J
D → A: $PV$ rises to 200 J, so $\Delta U = +150$ J; no work is done
The input energy is the sum of the positive values

slides.notes: Check: the sum of all four values of $Q$ is $1500 - 900 - 500 + 150 = 250$ J, which equals the net work.

points.guide: The Carnot cycle sets a limit for the efficiency of a heat engine at the temperatures of its heat reservoirs as given by η_Carnot = 1 − T_c/T_h.
aims: Describe the four stages of the Carnot cycle.
Calculate the Carnot efficiency, and use it as the upper limit for an engine.

slides.title: The Carnot cycle
bullets: An ideal, reversible cycle with four stages:
isothermal expansion at $T_h$: takes in $Q_h$
adiabatic expansion: cools from $T_h$ to $T_c$
isothermal compression at $T_c$: gives out $Q_c$
adiabatic compression: warms from $T_c$ to $T_h$
No engine working between the same two reservoirs can be more efficient
slides.notes: Ask which stages have zero $Q$ (the two adiabatic ones) and which have zero $\Delta U$ (the two isothermal ones).

slides.title: Carnot efficiency
bullets: $T_h$ and $T_c$ are the temperatures of the reservoirs, in kelvin

slides.title: Deriving the Carnot efficiency
slides.start: Start from the efficiency in terms of energy flows. The Carnot cycle has a special property that links them to temperature.

steps.text: In a Carnot cycle (shown later, using entropy)

slides.title: Using the Carnot efficiency
bullets: Always change Celsius temperatures to kelvin first
It is the upper limit: real engines fall below it because of friction, turbulence and heat leaks
It rises when the hot reservoir is hotter or the cold reservoir colder
It could reach 100% only with a cold reservoir at 0 K, which is impossible

slides.title: The Carnot cycle on a p–V graph
bullets: Two isotherms joined by two adiabats
The enclosed area is the net work per cycle

slides.title: A parabolic-trough solar engine
slides.question: An engine running on the Carnot cycle works between oil heated by parabolic-trough solar collectors, at 520 K, and the surrounding air at 300 K. In each cycle it takes in 2.6 kJ from the hot oil. Find (a) its efficiency, (b) the work done per cycle and (c) the thermal energy given out per cycle.
slides.hint: In a Carnot cycle, the two reservoir temperatures set the efficiency. Then efficiency links the work to the input energy.

steps.text: (c) The remaining energy is given out

slides.title: Power from the sea
slides.question: Ocean thermal power plants use warm surface water at 27 °C as the hot reservoir and deep water at 5 °C as the cold reservoir. Find (a) the maximum possible efficiency and (b) the minimum rate at which thermal energy must be taken from the warm water for an output of 1.0 MW.
slides.hint: Change both temperatures to kelvin. For (b), think about how efficiency links the useful power to the input power.

steps.text: Temperature of the warm water in kelvin

slides.notes: Real plants reach about 3%, so they must pump huge volumes of water. The fuel is free, which is why the idea is still attractive.

points.guide: The second law of thermodynamics refers to the change in entropy of an isolated system and sets constraints on possible physical processes and on the overall evolution of the system. (Guidance: Clausius and Kelvin forms, and entropy change in reversible and irreversible processes in isolated systems.)
aims: State the second law in its Kelvin, Clausius and entropy forms.
Explain how the second law limits what can happen to a system.

slides.title: The second law: three forms
bullets: Kelvin form: an engine working in a cycle can't convert all the thermal energy it takes in into work
Clausius form: thermal energy can't pass by itself from a colder body to a hotter one
Entropy form: the total entropy of an isolated system never decreases
The three forms are equivalent: if one failed, the others would too
slides.notes: The equivalence of these statements took decades of debate between scientists in several countries, which fits the "shared endeavour" aspect of NoS.

slides.title: What the second law forbids
bullets: Energy conservation alone doesn't settle the direction of a process: the second law does
A hot drink could gain energy from a cooler room without breaking the first law, but it never does
Every heat engine must have a cold reservoir, so its efficiency is below 100%
It lets us predict how an isolated system will change: towards higher entropy
If the universe is treated as an isolated system, its entropy must be increasing
slides.notes: Link to the guiding question on the future evolution of a system, and to E.5.

points.guide: Entropy S is a thermodynamic quantity that relates to the degree of disorder of the particles in a system.
aims: Describe entropy as a measure of the disorder of the particles in a system.
Compare the entropy of different states of a system.

slides.title: Entropy and disorder
bullets: Entropy $S$ tells us how disordered the particles of a system are; its unit is $\text{J K}^{-1}$
The more ways the particles can be arranged and share energy, the greater the entropy
For the same amount of a substance, entropy is higher:
for a liquid than for a solid, and for a gas than for a liquid
for a larger volume
at a higher temperature
An untidy room is a helpful picture: there are many more untidy arrangements than tidy ones
slides.notes: Ask: can the room become tidy again? Yes, but someone has to do work, and that person warms the surroundings. That leads directly to local decreases in entropy.

points.guide: Entropy can be determined in terms of macroscopic quantities such as thermal energy and temperature as given by ΔS = ΔQ/T and also in terms of the properties of individual particles of the system as given by S = k_B ln Ω, where k_B is the Boltzmann constant and Ω is the number of possible microstates of the system. (Guidance: microstates are equally probable; simple combinatorial model, for example coins.)
aims: Count microstates in a simple model, and calculate entropy using $S = k_B\ln\Omega$.
Calculate entropy changes using $\Delta S = \dfrac{\Delta Q}{T}$.

slides.title: Macrostates and microstates
bullets: Macrostate: the overall description, such as "3 heads out of 6 coins"
Microstate: one exact arrangement, saying which coin is which
Every microstate is equally likely
Mixed macrostates have far more microstates than tidy ones, so they are far more likely
In a gas, microstates can differ in the position, speed and direction of each particle
slides.notes: Toss six coins in groups and tally the results to see the pattern build up.

slides.title: Two ways to find entropy
bullets: $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant, and $\Omega$ is the number of microstates
$\Delta Q$ is the thermal energy transferred to the system at constant temperature $T$
slides.notes: Strictly, $\Delta Q$ is a reversible transfer; a body large enough to stay at a steady temperature can be treated this way. The logarithm makes entropies add when systems are combined, because their numbers of microstates multiply. With one possible microstate, $\ln 1 = 0$, so the entropy is zero.

slides.title: Entropy change from microstates
slides.start: A system changes from a macrostate with $\Omega_1$ microstates to one with $\Omega_2$.

slides.title: Why heat flows from hot to cold
slides.start: Thermal energy $Q$ passes from a large body at $T_h$ to a large body at $T_c$. Neither temperature changes noticeably. Together they form an isolated system.

steps.text: Entropy lost by the hot body
Entropy gained by the cold body
The cold body has the lower temperature, so the total increases. The opposite flow would decrease it, so the Clausius form agrees with the entropy form.

slides.title: The Carnot ratio from entropy
slides.start: In a Carnot cycle, thermal energy transfers only during the two isothermal stages, and every stage is reversible.

steps.text: Entropy gained by the gas at $T_h$
Entropy lost by the gas at $T_c$
The gas returns to its starting state, so its total change is zero

slides.notes: This completes the derivation of the Carnot efficiency. The adiabatic stages have $Q = 0$, so no entropy change.

slides.title: Using the entropy equations
bullets: Temperature must be in kelvin
Energy flowing out of a body gives that body a negative change in entropy
When energy passes between bodies, find each change and then add them
Phase changes are ideal uses of $\Delta S = \dfrac{\Delta Q}{T}$, as the temperature stays constant
Don't confuse $k_B$ with $\sigma$, the Stefan–Boltzmann constant

slides.title: Counting microstates
bullets: Ten coins, each landing heads or tails
The most mixed macrostate has the most microstates

slides.title: Eight gas molecules
slides.question: A box holds eight gas molecules, and each is equally likely to be in the left or the right half. (a) How many microstates does the macrostate "four on each side" have? (b) Find its entropy, counting only these left–right arrangements. (c) Find the probability of finding all eight molecules in the left half.
slides.hint: Each molecule behaves like a coin: left or right. How many ways are there to choose which four are on the left? Each microstate is equally likely.

steps.text: (a) Choose 4 of the 8 to be on the left
(c) The total number of microstates is
Only one microstate has all eight on the left

slides.notes: With $10^{23}$ molecules this probability becomes so small that it is never observed: a gas does not collect in one half of its container.

slides.title: Casting lead
slides.question: A foundry worker pours 3.0 kg of molten lead into a mould, where it solidifies at its melting point of 600 K. The specific latent heat of fusion of lead is $2.5 \times 10^{4}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}$. Find the change in entropy of the lead.
slides.hint: The temperature doesn't change during solidification. Is energy entering or leaving the lead? That gives the sign.

steps.text: Energy leaves the lead, so $\Delta Q$ is negative
The entropy of the lead falls

slides.notes: Ask how this can be allowed, given the second law. The surroundings gain more entropy than the lead loses, which comes up again with local decreases.

slides.title: Heat through a house wall
slides.question: On a winter day, thermal energy passes through the walls of a house at a rate of 2.0 kW, from the inside at 293 K to the outside air at 273 K. Find the total change in entropy of the inside and outside in each second.
slides.hint: In one second, 2000 J moves. Find the entropy change of each side separately, taking care with the signs, and then add them.
slides.notes: A positive total is what the second law requires for this flow. The two temperatures are close, so keep three significant figures in the intermediate values.

points.guide: Processes in real isolated systems are almost always irreversible and consequently the entropy of a real isolated system always increases.
aims: Distinguish between reversible and irreversible processes.
Use entropy changes to decide whether a proposed process is possible.

slides.title: Reversible or irreversible?
bullets: Reversible: an ideal process that could run backwards, leaving no change anywhere
In a reversible process, the total entropy of an isolated system stays constant
Irreversible: can't be undone without a change elsewhere; friction, turbulence and heat flow across a temperature difference are examples
In an irreversible process, the total entropy of an isolated system increases
Real processes are almost always irreversible, so a real isolated system gains entropy
slides.notes: Play a video of an egg breaking in reverse. Students notice at once that it is impossible, though no energy rule is broken.

slides.title: An inventor's claim
slides.question: An inventor claims that an engine working between reservoirs at 750 K and 310 K takes in 1000 J and does 620 J of work in each cycle. Use (a) the Carnot efficiency and (b) the entropy change of the two reservoirs to test the claim.
slides.hint: For (a), compare the claimed efficiency with the upper limit. For (b), use the first law to find the energy rejected, then find the entropy change of each reservoir.

steps.text: The upper limit is lower than this
Change in entropy of the two reservoirs
The total entropy would fall, so the claim is impossible

slides.notes: The engine's gas returns to its starting state, so its own entropy change over a cycle is zero. Only the reservoirs count.

points.guide: The entropy of a non-isolated system can decrease locally, but this is compensated by an equal or greater increase of the entropy of the surroundings.
aims: Explain how the entropy of a non-isolated system can decrease without breaking the second law.

slides.title: Entropy can fall locally
bullets: The second law applies to the total entropy of an isolated system
A non-isolated system can lose entropy if its surroundings gain at least as much
Making ice cubes: the water becomes more ordered, but the kitchen warms
Growing plants build ordered molecules using sunlight, and give out thermal energy
slides.notes: The room-tidying image returns here: a tidy room is a local decrease, paid for by the entropy increase caused by the person doing the tidying.

slides.title: Ice in a freezer
slides.question: A freezer turns 0.40 kg of water at 273 K into ice at 273 K. The motor does $4.0 \times 10^{4}$ J of work, and all the energy removed and the work done pass to the kitchen at 295 K. The specific latent heat of fusion of water is $3.34 \times 10^{5}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}$. Find (a) the entropy change of the water, (b) the entropy change of the kitchen and (c) the total.
slides.hint: Find the thermal energy removed from the water first. What is the total energy passed to the kitchen? Remember the signs.

steps.text: Energy to the kitchen includes the work

slides.notes: Ask: what is the smallest amount of work that would make the total exactly zero? That is the reversible limit.
